verses.note: The Spirit's first appearance in Scripture is at creation, present and active over what is not yet ordered. The Old Testament later speaks of the Spirit giving life (Psalm 104:30), a thread the New Testament picks up when it speaks of the Spirit's work of new creation.

The breath God gave in 2:7 is his to give and to withdraw. Human life depends moment by moment on God's Spirit (Psalm 104:29-30, Job 34:14-15), and this verse is the first time God says he will limit it.

In the Old Testament the Spirit of God gives wisdom, skill, and capacity to lead, not only prophecy. Pharaoh likely meant something within his own religion, but the narrator lets his words point to the true source of Joseph's gifts, as Nebuchadnezzar's words about Daniel will later do (Daniel 4:8).

Jeremiah does not name the Spirit, but Ezekiel's parallel promise joins the new heart to God's Spirit within (Ezekiel 36:26-27), and Paul reads the two together when he calls the Corinthians a letter written ‘with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts’ (2 Corinthians 3:3).

The Old Testament knew the Spirit coming on judges, prophets, and kings for particular tasks. Here the Spirit is promised to the whole people, permanently, within, and for ordinary obedience. That promise is what Joel 2:28-29 announces and what Peter declares fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16-18, 33).

The Spirit who will give life to the bones in verse 14 is first the Spirit who brings the prophet into the valley. The chapter begins and ends with God's Spirit acting: carrying the messenger, then raising the dead.

The Spirit is here the giver of life, the role the Nicene Creed confesses when it names the Holy Spirit as Lord and giver of life. Ezekiel ties the Spirit to both the new heart (36:26-27) and the raising of the dead, the two works Paul joins when he says the Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to believers' mortal bodies (Romans 8:11).
